title: Preparing the UK for a hotter climate
label: 18 November 2026 · Climate adaptation
summary: The Climate Change Committee told MPs that the UK is not prepared for the heat, flooding and other risks it already faces. Government planning has improved, but the witnesses said there is too little evidence of practical change. They called for measurable goals across departments, clearer information about spending and faster action, particularly to keep buildings cool.

chapters.title: The climate has already changed
chapters.takeaway: This summer's heat exposed risks to health, homes and essential services that the UK is not ready to manage.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How prepared is the UK for the climate we're experiencing now, and for what the next 10 to 20 years may bring?

evidence.quote: how well prepared is the UK for the climate impacts that we are already experiencing and for those that we anticipate experiencing over the next 10 to 20 years?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: We're not ready for the climate we already have. This summer England had five heatwaves, including one lasting 37 days. An initial assessment put heat-related deaths in May and June alone at almost 3,000. My own estimate is that the full summer figure could be nearer 5,000, but we don't have that figure yet.

evidence.quote: We had five heatwaves, one of which lasted 37 days in England.
The initial assessment of the number of heat-related deaths in May and June alone was that there were almost 3,000.
I would not be surprised if we see a number of excess heat-related deaths nearer to 5,000—now, that is my estimate
This summer has made it absolutely clear to us that we are not ready for the climate that has already arrived.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: The heat put pressure on hospitals, while drought brought hosepipe bans and wildfires. Rail journeys were disrupted, more than 1,000 schools closed in June because classrooms were too hot, and insurers reported a record number of claims for damage caused when ground beneath buildings shifted.

evidence.quote: It is putting our health system under pressure
We had a huge proportion of England under a hosepipe ban
That very hot and dry weather meant we had another record wildfire year
We have seen disruptions to the rail system—we have seen problems with rail buckling and problems with subsidence.
more than 1,000 schools closed in June because the temperatures in schools were too hot for children to learn and for teachers to teach.
The insurance industry reported that they have had the largest number of subsidence claims ever

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What should the Government tackle first?

evidence.quote: If you were to point to the biggest adaptation gaps that need to be filled, what would you cite as the key priorities for the Government?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: Heat needs far more attention. We expect 92% of homes to overheat by mid-century. This summer, some families in high-rise flats faced indoor temperatures of 40°C and had nowhere suitable to stay. We need to make existing homes, hospitals, schools and prisons safer in hot weather, and provide public places such as libraries where people can cool down.

evidence.quote: The one we have not spent anything like enough attention on in this country is heat
92% of homes in this country are predicted to overheat by mid-century.
young mums in flats in high-rise buildings where the temperatures inside were getting up to 40°C and they had nowhere to go.
dealing with our existing buildings, dealing with our existing hospitals, dealing with our schools, dealing with our prisons, and making sure there are public buildings, like public libraries

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are we taking heat-related deaths seriously enough? Thousands of families may have lost someone because we couldn't keep people safe in these temperatures.

evidence.quote: Have we taken that seriously enough?
families have been through funerals that would not have happened but for climate change and our inability to keep them safe in these temperatures.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: I don't think so. Part of the problem is that we don't see ourselves as a hot country. We need better advice for the public, but also buildings, neighbourhoods and places to go that are designed for hotter summers.

evidence.quote: I don’t think we are taking it seriously enough. I think one of the problems is cultural, in that we do not see ourselves as a hot country.

We need better engagement with the public and better information, but we also need to make sure we have buildings, communities and planning that account for higher temperatures, and the right places for people to go.

chapters.title: Plans need to become action
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses saw encouraging signs from ministers, but said departments must set goals, secure funding and show that conditions are improving.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: Where has the Government responded to your recommendations, and where is it still falling short?

evidence.quote: Where have the Government acted on those recommendations and where has their response been insufficient?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: In our 2025 report, we couldn't judge delivery to be good on any of the 46 results we examined. Government plans were improving, but we weren't yet seeing those plans make a difference. We're reassessing progress now, so I can't say what the next report will find.

evidence.quote: there were no adaptation outcomes, across the 46 outcomes we looked at, where we could assess that the delivery was good
planning is getting better—but we are not seeing the consequences of those plans.
we are in the process of repeating that analysis, so I cannot comment on it.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: There are positive signs. The Government has committed to plan for 2°C of warming by 2050 and told departments to set measurable goals. There's also more attention on wildfires. But the next national adaptation plan needs concrete goals and funding; ministerial interest alone won't make the changes happen.

evidence.quote: we have seen the Government commit that we will plan for 2° of warming by 2050 and that Government Departments have been told they must set measurable objectives
We have also recently seen an increased focus on wildfires.
We absolutely have to see concrete targets and plans in NAP4, and an indication that there is funding to support them

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: The next national adaptation plan isn't due until 2028. Should it come sooner, and what should happen meanwhile?

evidence.quote: The Government have decided to wait until 2028 to publish NAP4. What is your view on that? Should it be brought forward? What needs to happen in the meantime?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: That date follows the normal timetable; I wouldn't call it a delay. Departments shouldn't wait for the plan. They should set their goals now, ideally soon enough to ask for the money they need in the spending review, which comes first.

evidence.quote: 2028 is when NAP4 would be published in the normal cycle, as laid out in the Climate Change Act. There has not been a decision to delay it.
They do not have to await the NAP to do that. They should be doing that now.
Since the spending review comes before the NAP, it would be very good if they did them in time to get bids in for the spending review

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: How can the Government make departments work together on this, rather than leaving it to the environment department?

evidence.quote: what do you think is needed to drive the level of focus on climate and nature security and climate resilience up the Government agenda in a very cross-Government way?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: It needs stronger coordination across Government. A committee of ministers or a stronger role for the Cabinet Office could help. The environment department can't handle heat on its own: health, housing and education departments all have major parts to play.

evidence.quote: it needs strong cross-Government co-ordination.
We did once have a Cabinet sub-committee for climate change—a ministerial-level committee for co-ordinating climate change activity
There could be a stronger role for the Cabinet Office

it is very hard for DEFRA when so many of the requirements fall outside of its remit, particularly heat, for example. Heat falls under MHCLG, under the Department of Health and Social Care, under schools and education.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: If every department is responsible, who is accountable for making sure this happens?

evidence.quote: Who do you feel should be accountable for ensuring that we drive this forward?
if it is the responsibility of everybody, who is going to lead the charge, as it were?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: Every Secretary of State should be accountable for their department's goals and delivery. But the Prime Minister has to lead overall; he has shown he's willing to do that on wildfires.

evidence.quote: I think every Secretary of State should be accountable.
Secretaries of State in every Department need to know what their Department’s measurable objectives and targets are and make sure they are being delivered.
I think our Prime Minister has to do so, and he has shown that he is prepared to do that on wildfires.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: What about cooperation between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland?

evidence.quote: What about the roles of the devolved nations? How are they involved and how could we strengthen that further?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: Floods, fires and nature don't stop at borders. The four nations should coordinate better and report comparable information, though their priorities may rightly differ because they face different conditions.

evidence.quote: Nature does not stop at boundaries; rivers don’t stop at boundaries; floods don’t stop at boundaries. As you will hear from the fire chief, fires don’t stop at boundaries.
It would be very helpful if we had consistent data and reporting, because they all tend to report different types of data in slightly different ways with different definitions.
The different focus may be appropriate, because of course weather and climate impacts are different, depending on where you are.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: Which departments have engaged with you, and which haven't?

evidence.quote: Are you able to name which Departments are engaging with you and which have perhaps been less forthcoming when you have offered to meet?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: After our latest advice, we met ministers responsible for the environment, energy, defence and housing. Health, education, justice and the Treasury didn't take up our initial offer of ministerial meetings. Since the change of Prime Minister, we've met senior officials in the first three of those departments, and a Treasury ministerial meeting is now arranged.

evidence.quote: we met with Ministers from DEFRA, DESNZ, MOD and MHCLG, and our offer of meetings with Secretaries of State and Ministers was not taken up by the Department of Health and Social Care, the Department for Education, the Ministry of Justice and the Treasury.
subsequent to the change in Prime Minister, we have now met with senior civil servants in Health, Justice and Education.
We now have a meeting with the Treasury Exchequer Secretary in a couple of weeks’ time

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: We still haven't met the Department for Transport, among others. That's a significant gap. We'd also very much like health and education ministers themselves to engage, given the goals their departments must set and the funding they'll need.

evidence.quote: We have not yet met with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, the Department for Transport and the FCDO. Some of those I think are quite significant—for example, the Department for Transport.
We would very much like to see ministerial engagement and recognition by Ministers in those Departments that their Departments are supposed to be setting measurable objectives.
recognising the importance of the implications for their spending review bids.

chapters.title: Measuring progress and planning ahead
chapters.takeaway: Better evidence and plans for hotter conditions are needed, but even good plans must be followed by practical work.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: What information does the Government need to tell whether adaptation is working?

evidence.quote: What are the priority indicators that the Government should be focusing on as they amend their approach to measuring climate adaptation progress?

turns.speaker: Florence Bates
turns.text: There are major gaps. We don't have enough information about overheating in schools and care facilities, or about how widely cooling measures are being used. We also lack good evidence on weather damage to communications systems, effects on UK food production and prices, and harm to nature. National figures often aren't updated frequently enough.

evidence.quote: including instances of overheating in schools and also in key facilities such as in social care—where we do not have enough evidence or data on the uptake of key adaptation solutions, including cooling.
including in telecoms, for example, as well as the impact of climate change on domestic food production and food prices.
There is also a real dearth of data when it comes to the impact of climate change on our natural environment
the indicators are often not updated regularly enough on a national scale.

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: Is there an approach elsewhere that we could learn from?

evidence.quote: Is there anything we can learn from the approach of other countries?

turns.speaker: Florence Bates
turns.text: The next national adaptation plan should say how progress on its goals will be checked, with a public report each year. Scotland already does this alongside its adaptation plans.

evidence.quote: the fourth national adaptation programme to be accompanied by a monitoring evaluation framework that allows us to track progress against the measurable objectives
report progress annually in a published report that the public can see. That is something the Scottish Government have been doing

turns.speaker: John Whitby
turns.text: Is planning for 2°C of warming by 2050 enough, given how quickly temperatures are rising?

evidence.quote: If we are making the assumption of 2050 for 2°, are we comfortable we will not get there before that?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: The advice we've received says that's an appropriate starting point, and we should act now and review it as new evidence comes in. But we also wanted the Government to include a possible 4°C rise by the end of the century in its assessment of national risks. Long-lasting infrastructure, such as reservoirs and electricity systems, needs to be able to cope as conditions change.

evidence.quote: The best advice we have from our colleagues in the Met Office and other areas is that that is an appropriate target.
It is better to start planning for that and get moving now. We will keep that under review as time goes on and more data becomes available.
we should expect there to be 4° of warming on the risk register for the end of the century
We should be thinking, as we maintain that through its life, about how we would be able to cope with even significantly higher temperatures by the end of the century.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: The UN's latest estimate points towards 2.8°C by the end of the century. Do we understand what that would mean for essential services and infrastructure?

evidence.quote: The UN’s latest estimate is that we are heading for 2.8°. Do you think our country has an understanding of what adaptation, particularly in relation to our critical infrastructure, looks like if we hit 2.8°?
Of course, 2.8° is an end-of-century figure.

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: We need to update the temperatures that equipment and buildings are designed to withstand. In 2022, data centres supporting Guy's and St Thomas' hospital failed in the heat, disrupting patient appointments. Industries can't keep relying on design standards set decades ago, and changing those standards mustn't take ten years.

evidence.quote: When the data centres supporting Guy’s and St Thomas’ failed in the summer of 2022 and we lost all those patient appointments
a whole range of industries need to look at the standards they have worked to, in many cases, for the past 20 or 30 years and recognise that the climate has moved, but they have not moved.
it is no good if it takes 10 years to agree to change the standard.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Does the Department for Transport understand what it will cost to protect vulnerable transport routes? For example, the Fen line railway sits on peat that's drying out and shrinking.

evidence.quote: my constituency depends on the Fen line railway, which is sat on top of peat that is drying out and shrinking.

Do you think the Department for Transport understands the scale of the risk our infrastructure faces and what adapting to that looks like? Crucially, does the DFT have an adequate price tag in mind for what it needs to do?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: Transport is one area where plans for climate change have generally been good. That doesn't tell us whether enough money will be provided or the work done. We can't assess the Fen line itself: our team doesn't examine every railway. In our last assessment, transport planning was good, but putting those plans into practice wasn't.

evidence.quote: In general, in our assessments, the planning for climate change in the transport system is quite good.
that doesn’t mean that has been translated into what they are putting in for the spending review and whether the funding is going to be there
we do not get into the detail of every bit of railway line
the planning in the last assessment was good—I think that is true to say—but the implementation was not good.

chapters.title: What needs paying for
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses expect current spending to fall short, especially for cooling, but say the Government cannot yet identify clearly how much it spends on adaptation.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: The Government says it's providing £6.7 billion over nine years for urgent risks in NHS buildings, including cooling. Is that enough for the heat problem?

evidence.quote: The Government have told us that they are supporting the NHS with £6.7 billion over nine years to target the most critical estate risks, including cooling, to prepare for the extreme heat you have mentioned. Do you think that stacks up, relative to the magnitude of the problem our NHS is facing?

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: We don't know enough about how the larger sum will be spent to judge it. The identifiable amount for cooling, ventilation and some other work is £32 million, which doesn't look adequate.

evidence.quote: We do not have the detail of how that funding is going to be spent, so it is very hard to say.
When you get down to the figure of £32 million that was identified for cooling, ventilation and some other things, that does not look like an adequate sum of money.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Your estimate says about £11 billion a year is needed for adaptation. Are we spending enough?

evidence.quote: The Climate Change Committee report estimates that a total additional investment of around £11 billion per year, shared between public and private sectors, is required for us to be well adapted. Does the UK currently invest enough in climate adaptation relative to the scale of the risks it faces?

turns.speaker: Dr Richardson
turns.text: First, £11 billion is our estimate of total annual spending needed, not extra spending on top of what's already being done. We can't say precisely how much is being spent now, partly because the Government doesn't set it out clearly. But we are confident it isn't enough: cooling, flood protection and new reservoirs are all areas where more is needed.

evidence.quote: the £11 billion is the total of how much we think needs to be spent per year—it is not additional.
we are not able to identify with any certainty how much, particularly because the Government does not set that out.
Undoubtedly, though, it will not be enough.
particularly in areas around cooling.

although there is a flood budget, activity is taking place and we have been doing it for a long time, that budget is not at the scale needed. Similarly, there are activities happening to build new reservoirs and so on, but again it is not happening at the scale needed.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Where should spending go first?

evidence.quote: What kind of areas should the Government prioritise in their climate adaptation expenditure?

turns.speaker: Dr Richardson
turns.text: Cooling is the largest part of our estimate: about 35%, or just under £4 billion a year. It's probably also where the least is happening now. Flooding, water and transport are other big areas. Not every important step requires public spending, though: Flood Re, which helps people in flood-risk homes obtain insurance, is due to end in 2039, and a buyer needs to think about what happens after that.

evidence.quote: We think cooling is the largest area of that £11 billion. It is about 35%, so that is just shy of £4 billion that needs to be spent on that.
the area where the least activity is currently taking place. The other big areas are floods, water—which is mostly in the private sector in England, although not in the other nations—and transport.

The Flood Re scheme, which enables insurance for properties that are at risk of flooding, is due to end in 2039. That is not very far away if I am thinking about buying a property that relies on Flood Re to get my insurance. But that isn’t public expenditure.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: What costs are still missing from your estimate?

evidence.quote: Are there any significant gaps in adaptation funding? How should the Government prioritise investment anywhere else?

turns.speaker: Dr Richardson
turns.text: We couldn't put reliable figures on everything. For example, we lack good estimates for electricity, communications networks and local roads. Food supplies are harder still because they involve complex chains of businesses. The Government needs to understand whether those businesses are preparing and investing, even where it wouldn't be public money.

evidence.quote: That £11 billion figure covers the areas where we could identify the spending need.
we do not have a clear estimate on the energy system or the telecom system. We do not have a very good estimate on local roads

things like food security. It is very hard to understand what needs to be spent through these very complicated supply chains. That will not be a matter for the Government, but it is important that the Government understand whether that activity is taking place and whether resources are going into it.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Should the Government consider places to store food for people who can't build up supplies themselves, in case food supplies break down?

evidence.quote: Do you think we should have Nightingale-style places around the country where the Government are able to store food for those who cannot stockpile, in case of a breakdown?

turns.speaker: Dr Richardson
turns.text: Yes, it should examine that. We haven't reached a firm view on whether national food stores or stocks held by businesses would work better. The Government needs to identify where supplies could fail, compare the options and make a deliberate choice.

evidence.quote: We have said that is something we think the Government need to look at.
we have not been able to reach a definitive view on that and on the merits of, as it were, national stockpiling versus private stockpiling.
They need to understand what could go wrong and where the system could break, and they need to assess whether they are going to have national stockpiling approaches

turns.speaker: Baroness Brown of Cambridge
turns.text: They also need to understand what climate change could do to food prices, when many households are already under pressure from other costs.

evidence.quote: We think they also need a better understanding of the potential impact of climate change on food price inflation for the public, who are already very stressed in terms of the impact of a whole range of costs.
